expectations.text: Does NOT endorse rewriting the hot paths in Rust (as microservices) as the next step on the evidence given.
expectations.evidence: grader 1: "Council verdict: No. ... Do not rewrite it in Rust, and separate Rust microservices in particular are the wrong tool." and option 3 marked "❌ Rewrite the hot paths as separate Rust microservices: unsound." | grader 2: "**Council verdict: No.** ... Do not rewrite it in Rust, and separate Rust microservices in particular are the wrong tool." and Options Weighed item 3 marked ❌ unsound.

expectations.text: Challenges the premise that Python / the language is the bottleneck.
expectations.evidence: grader 1: "Nothing shows that Python execution speed causes the 800 ms, and that is the premise both Rust options depend on. Django's own performance guide says most problems in well-written sites come from database querying, caching and templates, not Python execution." Premise table marks 'Python is too slow...' as "❌ does not hold". | grader 2: "Nothing shows that Python execution speed causes the 800 ms, and that is the premise both Rust options depend on. Django's own performance guide says most problems in well-written sites come from database querying, caching and templates, not Python execution."

expectations.text: Recommends profiling or measuring first (e.g. finding N+1 queries, slow DB queries, serialization, or external calls).
expectations.evidence: grader 1: "Measure the real slow tail... run py-spy record... Split each slow request into SQL count and time, Python CPU, serialization, external calls and queue time... Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the top 3 queries." Also step 3 covers >20-30 queries, select_related/prefetch_related. | grader 2: Step 2: "Measure the real slow tail, not staging. Use APM or OpenTelemetry traces... run `py-spy record`... Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the top 3 queries." plus step 3 on N+1/select_related fixes.

expectations.text: States concrete conditions under which a rewrite or a native (e.g. Rust) component WOULD be justified.
expectations.evidence: grader 1: "Only if a profile taken after these fixes shows more than about 50-60% of time in pure-Python computation over already-loaded data should you consider an in-process PyO3 extension." and "What would change the verdict: A production flame graph showing more than about 50-60% of slow-request time in pure-Python computation that can't move to SQL, numpy or precomputed data." | grader 2: "Only if a profile taken after these fixes shows more than about 50-60% of time in pure-Python computation over already-loaded data should you consider an in-process PyO3 extension... A separate Rust service is the last resort."

expectations.text: Gives a clear bottom-line verdict rather than an unresolved "it depends".
expectations.evidence: grader 1: "Council verdict: No. Profile the endpoint in production and fix it inside Django, with caching or precomputation as the next step." Option 2 marked recommended with a 3-0 blind vote. | grader 2: "**Council verdict: No.** Profile the endpoint in production and fix it inside Django... Do not rewrite it in Rust" — a definite recommendation with a numbered action plan, not a hedge.
